newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN arms talks remain blocked.
newsitem.headline: UN arms talks remain blocked.

text.p: An international disarmament conference remained deadlocked on Thursday with little prospect of launching formal negotiations either to ban landmines or halt production of nuclear bomb-making material, diplomats said.
Demands by non-aligned countries, led by India and Pakistan, that nuclear powers set a calendar for total nuclear disarmament continue to tie up the United Nations forum, they added.

The world's five declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) back negotiations to halt production of bomb-making fissile material as the next step, but refuse to set up a committee on total nuclear disarmament.

Western states have also called for negotiations to agree a total ban on landmines, blamed for killing 25,000 people a year. But some states, including Mexico and Cuba, are reluctant to negotiate a total ban in the 61-member body, diplomats say.
"Things are deadlocked, the positions seem very tough," Russian disarmament ambassador Grigori Berdennikov told Reuters.
"As things stand now, it is very difficult to see where the solution lies," he added. "I hope the Group of 21 (non-aligned countries) can be reasonable."
A U.S. source told Reuters: "There is no daylight at this point. We're in a tunnel with no light at the end."

"The Group of 21 is still holding out for a nuclear disarmament committee," the U.S. source added. "Although they say that nuclear disarmament is their priority and there is no linkage on anti-personnel mines, it is effectively linkage."

Western diplomats say "some sort of package" will have to be found covering the three top areas: nuclear disarmament, fissile material and anti-personnel landmines. But they doubt a formula can be hammered out before the current session ends on March 27.
"It looks like linkage is the name of the game," said one.

Slovakia's ambassador Maria Krasnohorska, in a speech to Thursday's session, said: "We believe that such linkages are not plausible to be conducive, on the other hand there is a realistic threat that they will be counter-productive and endanger progress even on those items where it is possible."
She called for moving ahead with formal negotiations on both the fissile "cut-off" talks covering plutonium and highly-enriched uranium, as well as the landmines ban.
